redditSourcedNotes: No Reddit or other community content was obtained for Mexico City: the research stage ran with the session's WebSearch budget already exhausted and every fetch fallback egress-blocked, so the draft came from the researcher's own knowledge with empty sources. The verify stage had a budget of 5 searches and spent them on the highest-doubt items: four unconfirmed English Wikipedia titles and one existence/hours check (Parque Masayoshi Ohira). Results: 'Biblioteca de México' corrected to the confirmed article 'Biblioteca de México José Vasconcelos'; 'Kiosco Morisco' corrected to the confirmed article 'Morisco Kiosk'; 'Espacio Escultórico' and Parque Ecológico de Xochimilco set to null because only Spanish Wikipedia / Wikidata pages surfaced; Parque Masayoshi Ohira confirmed as an open, free public park (official CDMX venue page; hours reported 8am-9pm) and its unsupported '2023 restoration' claim removed. The remaining four titles (Biblioteca Vasconcelos, Viveros de Coyoacán, Tepeyac, Desierto de los Leones National Park) were kept from the reviewer's own knowledge of well-established articles and are flagged as unconfirmed in each verifyNote. Sources were added only where the URL actually appeared in one of the five search results; spots without a search still have empty sources. All 14 draft spots are real, long-established public places and were kept; no spot needed dropping for safety, but four keep a caution level (Espacio Escultórico, Kiosco Morisco plaza after 10pm, Parque Ecológico de Xochimilco, Desierto de los Leones). Hours remain from memory where marked 'check'. Re-run with search capacity to add r/MexicoCity opinions and confirm the four unchecked Wikipedia titles.

spots.name: Biblioteca Vasconcelos
spots.blurb: A cathedral-sized public library where steel shelves hang in tiers above a long central nave and Gabriel Orozco's whale skeleton floats over the reading tables. You take any seat on the upper walkways, read or work for hours, and nobody bothers you; outside, a botanical garden wraps the building with paths and benches that most visitors skip.
spots.tips: Head to the top floors at the far end for the emptiest desks, then take a book out to the garden benches. Bring ID if you want to use the computers; weekday mornings are near silent, Sunday afternoons fill with families.

safety.note: Staffed, busy public building next to Buenavista station; the surrounding streets are fine by day and quieter after dark, so leave when it closes.

spots.verifyNote: Well-known public library; not searched (budget spent on doubtful items). Wikipedia title kept from reviewer knowledge, not confirmed live. Hours from memory.

spots.name: Biblioteca de México (La Ciudadela)
spots.blurb: An 18th-century tobacco factory turned citadel turned public library, with sunlit stone courtyards, columned arcades and a series of reading rooms built around the personal libraries of writers such as Carlos Monsiváis and José Luis Martínez. It is far calmer than Vasconcelos: you can sit in a courtyard with a book, drift into a reading room, and hear little but pages turning.
spots.tips: Enter from Plaza de la Ciudadela (Metro Balderas) and look for the writers' library rooms on the ground floor; the courtyard benches are the place for a slow hour. The craft market across the plaza is handy for a cheap lunch.

sources.label: Biblioteca de México (Secretaría de Cultura) official site
Mexico City government: La Ciudadela, Library of Mexico
Time Out México: secrets of La Ciudadela / Biblioteca de México

safety.note: Staffed building on a busy plaza; leave by closing time, as the streets around Balderas empty out after dark.

spots.verifyNote: Existence confirmed by search (official site, CDMX venue page). Wikipedia title corrected to the confirmed English article 'Biblioteca de México José Vasconcelos'. Hours from memory.

spots.name: Librería Rosario Castellanos (Centro Cultural Bella Época)
spots.blurb: A 1940s cinema converted by the Fondo de Cultura Económica into one of the biggest bookshops in the city, with a glass ceiling by Jan Hendrix, a small art-house cinema and a café at the back. Locals treat it as a public living room: pick a book, take a chair or a café table, and stay a while without being hurried.
spots.tips: Café tables near the back are the quietest; the children's corner and front tables get busy on weekends. It opens into the evening, so it works as a rainy-night refuge after a walk around Parque México.

safety.note: Well-lit Condesa corner with restaurants all around; comfortable at night.

spots.verifyNote: Well-known FCE bookshop on Tamaulipas; not searched. 'Stay as long as you like without buying' softened. Hours from memory.

spots.name: Cafebrería El Péndulo Polanco
spots.blurb: A book-lined café with a plant-filled double-height atrium, tables tucked between the shelves and a mezzanine where people read and work for hours. It is calmer than the Condesa branch and a block from Parque Lincoln, so you can pair a coffee here with a bench by the park's little pond and aviary.
spots.tips: Upstairs tables by the railing are the quiet ones; weekday mornings are the emptiest. Order a coffee and nobody minds if you stay through lunch.

safety.note: Polanco streets are well-lit and busy into the evening.

spots.verifyNote: Long-running branch on Alejandro Dumas; not searched. Hours from memory.

spots.name: Audiorama de Chapultepec
spots.blurb: A small walled garden tucked into the slope of the castle hill, where classical or ambient music plays softly over speakers and a few dozen people sit on benches and steps to read, nap or just listen. It has a small lending shelf of books and a rule of silence, which makes it feel like a secret inside the busiest park in the city.
spots.tips: Find it at the foot of the hill behind the castle, near the Baños de Moctezuma; ask a park guard for 'el Audiorama' if you get lost. Weekday afternoons are almost empty, and it shuts with the first section on Mondays.
spots.hours: Tue-Sun roughly 9am-4:30pm (closed Mon with the 1st section; check)

safety.note: Inside the fenced first section of the park with guards nearby; it closes well before dusk.

spots.verifyNote: Established park feature; not searched. Coordinates nudged toward the north foot of the castle hill by the Baños de Moctezuma; still medium confidence. Hours from memory.

spots.name: Parque Masayoshi Ōhira
spots.blurb: A Japanese garden in a residential corner of Coyoacán, with a koi pond, stone lanterns, a torii and cherry trees that flower briefly in early spring. Remodelled with help from the Mexican-Japanese community, it is a neighbourhood favourite for slow laps of the pond and quiet mornings on the benches.
spots.tips: Come on a weekday morning when the light is on the pond and the paths are empty; weekends bring families and photographers. Metro General Anaya is the nearest station.

sources.label: Mexico City government: Parque Masayoshi Ohira
México Ruta Mágica: history, how to get there, hours

safety.note: Quiet residential streets; the park is fenced and closes in the evening.

spots.verifyNote: Existence and free entry confirmed by search (official CDMX page, es.wikipedia); hours reported as 8am-9pm, replacing the draft's guess. Draft's '2023 restoration' not supported (sources cite a 2014 remodel), so the date was removed and 'few outsiders know it' softened. No English Wikipedia article surfaced.

spots.name: Viveros de Coyoacán
spots.blurb: A working tree nursery that doubles as a forest park, with straight shaded lanes between rows of cedars and eucalyptus and famously bold squirrels. Locals run the outer loop at dawn, then it settles into a calm of tai chi groups, readers on the low walls and people simply walking in the shade.
spots.tips: Enter from Avenida Universidad next to Metro Viveros and head for the inner nursery beds, which are the quietest. It closes early in the evening, so this is a morning or lunchtime spot.

safety.note: Fenced, busy and staffed throughout opening hours.

spots.verifyNote: Well-known national park/nursery; not searched. Wikipedia title kept from reviewer knowledge, not confirmed live.

spots.name: Plaza Luis Cabrera
spots.blurb: A small tree-shaded plaza around a set of fountains on Calle Orizaba, a few blocks from the busier Plaza Río de Janeiro. Neighbours sit on the benches with coffee or a book, dogs cool off in the fountain spray, and in the evening the surrounding restaurants leave it lit and lively without being loud.
spots.tips: Benches on the west side get the late sun; the cafés on the corners will do a coffee to go. It stays comfortable well into the evening but empties after midnight.

safety.note: Well-lit with restaurants around it; fine until late evening, quieter after midnight.

spots.verifyNote: Established Roma Norte plaza; not searched. No English Wikipedia article known.

spots.name: Espacio Escultórico UNAM
spots.blurb: A ring of 64 concrete prisms, 120 metres across, set around a field of black volcanic rock from the Xitle eruption on the edge of the UNAM cultural centre. Students come to sit on the rim in the late afternoon, when the lava turns copper and the Ajusco hills go purple, and the scale of the space makes even a small crowd feel like solitude.
spots.tips: Reach it from the Centro Cultural Universitario car park past the MUAC. Stay on the ring and the paths; the lava field inside is a protected ecological reserve. Go on a weekday late afternoon and leave before dark, when the campus paths empty.

sources.label: UNAM Global: Espacio Escultórico, an artistic and historic jewel of UNAM
Fundación UNAM: get to know the Espacio Escultórico
Time Out México: Espacio Escultórico de la UNAM

safety.note: Open campus land with no lighting; visit in daylight, leave before dusk, and ideally go with a friend.

spots.verifyNote: Existence and public access confirmed by search (UNAM sources, Time Out). Only the Spanish Wikipedia article surfaced, so wikipediaTitle set to null. Tip encouraging scrambling onto the lava removed; it is a protected reserve.

spots.name: Alameda de Santa María la Ribera (Kiosco Morisco)
spots.blurb: An old-fashioned neighbourhood square built around the Kiosco Morisco, a Moorish-style iron pavilion made for the 1884 New Orleans exposition and re-erected here in 1910. Families and old men on benches, dance classes under the kiosk on weekend evenings and cheap cafés on the surrounding streets make it the kind of plaza where sitting for an hour is the whole activity.
spots.tips: Benches on the east side catch the last light on the kiosk's coloured glass. Pair it with a coffee on Calle Salvador Díaz Mirón; weekend afternoons are the liveliest.

sources.label: Mexico City government: Kiosco Morisco and the Alameda de Santa María
México Desconocido: the Kiosco Morisco of Santa María la Ribera
AFAR: Kiosco Morisco of Santa María la Ribera

safety.note: Busy and well-lit into the evening; the side streets get quiet late, so after about 10pm go with a friend or take a taxi.

spots.verifyNote: Confirmed by search; Wikipedia title corrected from 'Kiosco Morisco' to the confirmed English article 'Morisco Kiosk'. Kiosk history in blurb corrected to match sources (1884 New Orleans exposition, reopened here 1910).

spots.name: Jardines del Cerro del Tepeyac
spots.blurb: The landscaped hill behind the Basílica de Guadalupe, climbed by stone stairways past waterfalls and sculpture groups to the little Capilla del Cerrito at the top. The pilgrims mostly stay below in the atrium, so up here it is a few people on benches looking out over the north of the city and, on a clear morning, the volcanoes.
spots.tips: Go early on a weekday for clean air and views toward Popocatépetl; avoid December 12 and the days around it, when the whole hill is packed. The stairways close before the basilica does.
spots.hours: Roughly 7am-6pm (gardens close before the basilica; check)

safety.note: Patrolled sanctuary grounds, busy by day; leave with the crowds when the gardens close.

spots.verifyNote: Well-known sanctuary hill; not searched. 'Tepeyac' is the English article on the hill itself, kept from reviewer knowledge, not confirmed live.

spots.name: Parque Ecológico de Xochimilco
spots.blurb: A 148-hectare wetland park on the north edge of the Xochimilco canals, opened in 1993, with lagoons, reed beds, herons and a long lakeside path far from the party trajineras. You can rent a bike or simply walk to the far lake and sit on the bank, where the only sound is birds and the occasional canoe from the rowing course next door.
spots.tips: Enter from Periférico Oriente near the Cuemanco flower market; mornings are coolest and best for birds. Bring water and sun protection, as there is little shade along the path.

sources.label: SEDEMA CDMX: Parque Ecológico de Xochimilco (protected natural area)
Asociación Nacional de Parques y Recreación: Parque Ecológico de Xochimilco

safety.note: Large and sparsely staffed; stay on the main lakeside path, go with a friend on quiet weekdays and leave before closing.

spots.verifyNote: Existence confirmed by search (SEDEMA, WWF, es.wikipedia). Only Spanish Wikipedia / Wikidata surfaced, so wikipediaTitle set to null. Opening days/hours and free pedestrian entry not confirmed; hours left as 'check'.

spots.name: Finca Don Porfirio (Sears rooftop café)
spots.blurb: A plain café on the eighth floor of the Sears department store whose terrace looks straight down onto the orange dome of the Palacio de Bellas Artes and across the Alameda. Tourists know it, but it is still just a coffee and a chair with one of the best views in the city, and after the day-trippers leave it goes quiet.
spots.tips: Take the lift to the 8th floor and ask for a terrace table; late afternoon on a weekday has the shortest wait. Order a coffee and stay through dusk, when Bellas Artes lights up.

safety.note: Inside a department store on a busy, well-lit corner; the surrounding Centro streets stay busy until about 10pm.

spots.verifyNote: Well-known café; not searched. Hours from memory.

spots.name: Desierto de los Leones
spots.blurb: A cool pine and oyamel forest some 800 metres above the city, with a former 17th-century Carmelite monastery, mossy hermitages and soft trails along streams. Chilangos drive up on weekends for a walk and a quesadilla at the stalls, then sit on the monastery lawns; on a weekday you can have whole stretches of forest to yourself.
spots.tips: Take the short loop past the hermitages behind the convent for the quietest walk, and bring a layer since it is noticeably colder than the city. Weekday mornings are near empty; summer afternoons turn foggy and wet.
spots.wikipediaTitle: Desierto de los Leones National Park

safety.note: Stay on the main trails near the monastery and go with a friend on quiet weekdays; the forest closes at 5pm and there is no lighting.

spots.verifyNote: Well-known national park; not searched. Wikipedia title kept from reviewer knowledge, not confirmed live. Hours from memory.
